messages.subject: R2 for composite variables
parts:
Hello community,

I have a simple question about composite variables. I have a model that successfully converges,  produces an acceptable model P value and contains a composite variable. However, there is no R2 reported for the composite variables, which has two explanatory variables. Is this simply a fundamental aspect about composite variables or is there a procedure to determine the explained variation?

Thanks so much,
Jon

messages.subject: Re: R2 for composite variables
parts:
My apologies, I miss-specified the error. The R2 reported for the composite variable is 1. Is this a result of forcing the coefficient on one of the components to 1?


Syntax

SEM.composite = "
# Composite
   Filter <~1*Hmax + LMA

# Regression
   Filter ~NH4 + GWC
   FD ~Filter + Nleaf + GWC

  mean.D ~Filter + Nleaf
  density ~ Filter

  biomass ~ mean.D + density + Filter + Nleaf
  gain ~ biomass + density + Filter + FD + Nleaf + GWC "

SEM.fit = sem(SEM.composite, data, fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(SEM.fit, rsq = T, standardized = T)

# R2 outputs
FD + 0.688
mean.D = 0.237
density = 0.584
biomass = 0.718
gain = 0.447
Filter = 1.00

parts: Hi,

On 14 Aug 2017, at 15:27 , Jon S <jsschu...@gmail.com> wrote:

My apologies, I miss-specified the error. The R2 reported for the composite variable is 1. Is this a result of forcing the coefficient on one of the components to 1?
Not directly. It follows from the definition of a composite as a weighted use of the component variables.

Syntax

SEM.composite = "
# Composite
   Filter <~1*Hmax + LMA

# Regression
   Filter ~NH4 + GWC

Note that these two lines are equivalent to specifying:

 Filter <~1*Hmax + LMA + NH4 + GWC

So filter is a composite of four variables

FD ~Filter + Nleaf + GWC

  mean.D ~Filter + Nleaf
  density ~ Filter

Here you specify Filter as a common factor of mean.D and density, which (partially) allows you to define the composite weights.

Not sure if this is what you intended.

Mikko

biomass ~ mean.D + density + Filter + Nleaf
  gain ~ biomass + density + Filter + FD + Nleaf + GWC “


SEM.fit = sem(SEM.composite, data, fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(SEM.fit, rsq = T, standardized = T)

# R2 outputs
FD + 0.688
mean.D = 0.237
density = 0.584
biomass = 0.718
gain = 0.447
Filter = 1.00

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: R2 for composite variables
parts:
R2 = 1 is the result of forcing residual variance to 0.

You used the "formative" operator here:
Filter <~1*Hmax + LMA
(which is not a good idea--it's buggy)
If Filter is a simple composite of Hmax and LMA, then there is nothing else in Filter to explain--it is an exact function of Hmax and LMA.

I believe that what you want is to use this line:
  Filter ~NH4 + GWC
to run a regression with NH4 and GWC predicting the composite of Hmax and LMA. But SEM doesn't work ike that. There is only 1 equation per dependent variable. So the method somehow combines your 2 lines of syntax into 1 equation.
Look at your output--what is the actual formula for Filter, according to the output?
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: R2 for composite variables
parts:
Well, that's confusing. It does make it seem like there are two separate equations--when there *can't* be, because this is a factor-based package. My guess is that the mathematical reality is that Filter is a composite of 4 variables with 0 residual variance, which is not what you intend.
     lavaan estimates a factor-based model. In such a model, each unobserved variable is defined by covariances among its dependents, subject to constraints like the zero residual variance constraint. Your composite, Filter, has many dependents--it predicts DF, mean.D, density, biomass and gain. These variables have other dependents, some of which compose Filter, so the situation is not simple.
      You can try relaxing the 0 residual variance assumption, but that would then make Filter a common factor defined by its dependents and predicted by (not composed of) Hmax, LMA, NH4 and GWC. Such a model may or may not be statistically identified, but it still won't get you what you want, which is an "optimally" weighted composite of Hmax and LMA predicted by NH4 and GWC.
     What you might consider, if you want to continue with factor-based methods, is to form your own composite of Hmax and LMA outside the  model, and then use that composite as a variable inside the model--leaving out Hmax and LMA. You don't use them anywhere else in the model, so it seems the loss would be small. You might (easily) create a range of composites, using different weights, to see if it makes any difference. If sample size is small and the components are highly correlated, any difference will be small, possibly swallowed up in residual variance.
     An alternative would be to use some composite-based method to estimate your model, but some people object to composite-based approaches.
--Ed Rigdon
